Field test · 16 Oct 2026

Agent Substrate, frozen and thawed

Google's open-source runtime freezes idle AI agents into a storage bucket and thaws them onto any free machine. We stood it up on GKE from nothing, ran real Claude Code agents on it, checked its security claims, benchmarked it with its own harness and priced it against hosted sandboxes.

substrate @ 603e006 (after v0.5.0) · GKE 1.36.4 · 2 × c3-standard-4 · gVisor and microVM · us-west1 · ≈ $3 total

Setup, tests, raw data and teardown: github.com/shivanathd/agent-substrate-field-test

0.22 swake, small agent (median)
3.50 swake at 1 GiB
6.90 swake at 2 GiB (microVM 16.0 s)
4,717benchmark requests, 0 failed

What held up

Holds
State survives a freeze

20 of 20 cycles came back with memory, files and root filesystem exact, across three different workers.

Holds
Real coding agents can be frozen mid-task

Three Claude Code agents resumed with their in-memory loop counters intact, one on a different node, and kept getting answers from Claude.

Partly
“Sub-500 ms resume”

True for a small agent (0.22 s). A 1 GiB agent takes 3.50 s; a 2 GiB agent 6.90 s, or 16.0 s under microVM isolation.

Holds
Oversubscription without errors

15 agents on 10 workers: 2,123 requests, zero failures. Sleep slows down under load; wake barely moves.

Holds
Agents can use keys they never hold

The egress gateway injected a secret into an outbound request; the secret was nowhere in the agent's environment, processes or filesystem.

Fails
Secrets an agent does hold are safe at rest

Memory snapshots are not encrypted. The demo's API key was in them 77 times.

Depends
Cheaper than the alternatives

9× cheaper than one pod per agent at 5% awake. But a hosted sandbox that doesn't bill while paused (E2B: $1,511/month) beats Substrate on on-demand nodes ($2,303); Substrate wins on spot nodes ($1,056).

Who should care

  • Hundreds of stateful, mostly idle agents (one per user, customer or ticket) on a team that already runs Kubernetes: the core works today and the economics hold below about 25% awake.
  • A handful of agents, or busy ones: a Deployment or a hosted sandbox is simpler and no more expensive.
  • Everyone: inject credentials at the edge instead of handing them to agents. Snapshots keep whatever an agent holds.

Not a scale test (two nodes), not a production review, not affiliated with the Substrate project or Google.

How these were measured

Upstream's own Locust harness, running in-cluster as a Kubernetes Job, so no laptop or WAN in the path. Each run is an unmodified entry from upstream's benchmark catalogue; the memory entries were also run for 5 minutes instead of 1 because a 2 GiB agent only fits a few cycles a minute. glutton holds a fixed amount of memory and re-reads all of it after every wake, the worst case for lazy page loading. 18 runs, 4,717 requests, 0 failures.

Memory decides how long a wake takes

Budget about 3.5 s per GiB, with a long tail past 1 GiB: at 2 GiB one wake in twenty took 15 s on gVisor.

gVisor and microVM, side by side

1 GiBmicroVM233.50 s / 4.10 s / 8.40 s3.70 s / 4.30 s / 7.60 s2.55 s0.84 s
2 GiBgVisor136.90 s / 15.0 s / 15.0 s10.0 s / 18.0 s / 18.0 s4.96 s1.77 s
2 GiBmicroVM816.0 s / 17.0 s / 17.0 s11.0 s / 13.0 s / 13.0 s6.47 s9.54 s

Same at the median at 1 GiB, with microVM carrying the heavier tail. At 2 GiB microVM wakes take more than twice as long, and the difference is the sandbox restore itself, not the bucket. Stronger isolation is cheap for small agents and expensive for big ones.

What this test cost

$0.53per hour, cluster up
$12.73per day if left running
≈ $3the whole test day
4 h 15 mwall clock, start to last benchmark

Two c3-standard-4 nodes at $0.2153/h each including disk, plus the $0.10/h cluster fee. The expensive resource was time: about 1 h 30 m of it was image builds and downloads through the laptop.

1,000 agents a month, five ways

Each agent gets 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB when awake. Substrate needs enough nodes for the agents awake at once with 2× headroom, plus one for the control plane. Hosted sandboxes bill per second while running.

  • Against one pod per agent, Substrate is 9× cheaper at 5% awake, 2× at 25%, and no cheaper at 50%.
  • Against hosted sandboxes that stop billing when paused (E2B, Daytona), Substrate on on-demand nodes costs more at every duty cycle we modelled. Hosted pricing has no headroom or control-plane overhead.
  • Substrate wins on spot nodes (about 60% off), which suit it because agents already live in snapshots. We did not test spot: a reclaimed node leaves its agents CRASHED until reverted.
  • What the numbers leave out: running Postgres, the router, the gateway and node agents yourself; committed-use discounts; data residency and VPC control, which are the usual reasons to self-host.

Snapshot storage and bucket operations add about $30/month at 20 wakes per agent per day. An idle Claude Code agent's own snapshot was about 300 KB on top of an 18 MB base shared by its template.

What we ran

A request reaches an agent through the router, which wakes it onto a worker pod if it is asleep. The node agent checkpoints and restores agents to the bucket. Every outbound connection goes through the egress gateway, which enforces the allow-list and injects credentials.

How the test ran, including what broke

From an empty GCP project to published results. The bottom lane is every failure we hit and how it was fixed.

Run it yourself

# about $0.53 an hour while the cluster is up
cp scripts/env.example.sh scripts/env.sh     # new project ID, billing account
scripts/setup.sh                             # 45–60 min from nothing
tests/01-state-persistence.sh                # state survives 20 freeze/thaw cycles
tests/05-credential-injection.sh             # 8 checks incl. controls
tests/03-claude-multiplex.sh                 # needs an Anthropic key
bench/run-all.sh && bench/summarize.py       # 1–2 h of upstream benchmarks
python3 report/build_report.py               # this page
scripts/verify.sh --forbid <your-project>    # gate before publishing
scripts/teardown.sh --delete-project         # verifies nothing billable is left

Setup refuses to touch a project or Substrate checkout it did not create, and teardown refuses any project without its label. Run it from a cloud VM in the same region and most of the build and download time disappears.

Credentials injected at the edge

A random secret went into a Kubernetes Secret. The agent called an in-cluster echo server with Authorization: placeholder. Eight checks, all passed:

  • The server received Bearer <secret> and never saw the placeholder.
  • The request arrived from the egress gateway pod's IP, not the agent's.
  • The secret was absent from the agent's environment, every /proc/*/environ, and a full filesystem search (which we confirmed actually ran).
  • HTTPS to a host the policy doesn't cover was refused, and the same request succeeded once the policy allowed it, so the policy did the refusing.

An agent with no egress policy has all traffic blocked, DNS included. That is why the upstream Claude Code demo can't reach Claude as shipped.

Snapshots are RAM in a bucket

A memory snapshot is the agent's memory, compressed and written to object storage. Substrate does not encrypt it. The upstream demo passes its API key as an environment variable, so we unwrapped its snapshots and counted.

41 54 45 53 50 52 53 45 02 00 00 00 28 b5 2f fd …   ATESPRSE v2  zstd frame

Every snapshot object starts like this: an 8-byte magic, a version, then a plain zstd stream.

  • 77 copies of the full key across 12 snapshot objects: the template's shared base image, each agent's own delta, and checkpoint metadata.
  • Read access to the bucket is read access to every secret any agent held in memory.
  • Fix: inject credentials at the gateway so agents never hold them, and treat the bucket as a secret store anyway (customer-managed keys, tight IAM, access logs).

Other rough edges

  • Alpine-based agents couldn't resolve example.com inside the sandbox; example.com. with a trailing dot worked. Node-based agents were fine.
  • When a worker pod disappears, its agents go to CRASHED and wait for a manual revert.
  • Every image builds from source on the operator's machine; on Apple silicon that is amd64 under emulation.
  • The microVM installer needs a zstd binary it doesn't list, and finds out after a 924 MB download.

Nine items, with reproduction steps, are written up for the maintainers in docs/upstream-issues.md.

The publish gate

scripts/verify.sh must pass before anything is published. Independent code review

A separate reviewer read every script before publication. 23 findings: 3 high, 9 medium, 10 low, 1 open note. 22 fixed. The open note is honest about scope: setup.sh has not been run end to end; it was assembled from steps that were each run during the test.

Prices (read 16 Oct 2026)

  1. GCP Compute, GKE and Cloud Storage: Cloud Billing Catalog API for us-west1 (C3 on-demand and spot core/RAM, GCS Standard), plus disk pricing, GKE pricing and Cloud Storage pricing.
  2. E2B pricing: $0.000014 per vCPU-second, $0.0000045 per GiB-second. E2B billing FAQ: "Paused and killed sandboxes are not billed." E2B persistence: pause about 4 s per GiB, resume about 1 s (vendor figures, not measured here).
  3. Daytona pricing: $0.0504 per vCPU-hour, $0.0162 per GiB-hour, storage $0.000108 per GiB-hour after 5 GiB.
  4. Vercel Sandbox pricing: $0.128 per active CPU-hour, $0.0212 per provisioned GB-hour, snapshots $0.08 per GB-month.
  5. Modal and Cloudflare sandbox prices were found only in third-party comparisons and are left out.

Post kit

Everything a writer needs for the post, in this one file. The whole report is self-contained (fonts, charts and diagrams are inlined, nothing loads from the network), so the saved HTML can be handed to a writing agent as is. The same file is report/index.html in the repo.

Brief for the writer

  • Angle: a hands-on test of a new open-source agent runtime's claims, with numbers, by someone who ran real coding agents on it. Not a launch announcement or a tutorial.
  • Audience: engineering leads and platform engineers deciding how to host many AI agents; people who know Kubernetes but not Substrate.
  • The one idea to land: the economics depend on one number, the share of time agents are awake. Cheap below about 25%, no saving at 50%, and hosted sandboxes that don't bill while paused beat it on on-demand nodes.
  • The memorable moment: three Claude Code agents frozen mid-task, moved to other machines, and resumed with their in-memory counters intact.
  • The warning: memory snapshots are not encrypted; the upstream demo's API key was in them 77 times. The fix (gateway credential injection) works and was verified.
  • Call to action: the repo has setup, tests, raw data and teardown; invite people to run it on other hardware and share numbers.

Keep these true

  • Two nodes, one region, one day. It is not a scale test or a production review.
  • Spot nodes were priced, not tested. Costs are list prices on 16 Oct 2026.
  • Tested upstream commit 603e006; the project is pre-1.0 and changes weekly.
  • Not affiliated with the Substrate project or Google. "Sub-500 ms resume" holds for small agents only.
  • Use the exact numbers in the fact sheet below; don't round 3.5 s to "a few seconds" or 77 to "dozens".

LinkedIn draft

1,582 characters (LinkedIn allows 3,000)
I froze three Claude Code agents mid-task, moved one to a different machine, and woke them up. None of them noticed.

That's Agent Substrate, Google's new open-source runtime for running agents on Kubernetes. Idle agents get snapshotted to a bucket and thawed onto whatever machine is free. I spent a day testing it on GKE for about $3. What held up:

→ State survived 20 out of 20 freeze/thaw cycles, across machines
→ Wake-up is about 0.2 s for a small agent. For a 1 GB agent it's 3.5 s, and 7 s at 2 GB (16 s with microVM isolation). Memory size is everything.
→ 15 agents on 10 workers: 2,123 requests, zero failures
→ API keys can be injected at the gateway so the agent never holds them. I checked; it doesn't.

What didn't:

→ Memory snapshots aren't encrypted. The official demo's API key was sitting in them 77 times.
→ The Claude Code demo can't reach Claude out of the box (deny-by-default egress, no policy).
→ The install builds everything from source on your laptop. Slow on a Mac.

The economics come down to one number: how much of the time your agents are awake. For 1,000 agents awake 5% of the time it's roughly 9x cheaper than one pod per agent. By 50% the saving is gone.

The surprise: hosted sandboxes that don't bill while paused (E2B, Daytona) came in cheaper than self-hosting on on-demand nodes at every duty cycle I modelled. Self-hosting only wins on spot nodes. Run it for control, not price.

Setup, tests, raw data and teardown are open source: https://github.com/shivanathd/agent-substrate-field-test

#AIagents #Kubernetes #ClaudeCode #OpenSource

Long-form draft

# I put Claude Code agents to sleep on Google's Agent Substrate. Here's what woke up.

Agent Substrate is Google's new open-source runtime for running agents on Kubernetes. The pitch:
most agents sit idle most of the time, so instead of one pod per agent, freeze each one to object
storage when it goes quiet and thaw it onto any free machine when work arrives. Millions of
sandboxes, sub-500 ms resume, secure by default.

I wanted to know which of those claims survive contact with a real cluster and a real coding
agent. So I stood it up from nothing on GKE, ran three Claude Code agents on it, attacked its
security story, and benchmarked it with its own harness. Total spend: about $3. Total time: one
working day, a lot of it waiting for Docker.

Everything is reproducible: https://github.com/shivanathd/agent-substrate-field-test. Here's what I found.

## The core trick works

I froze and thawed a stateful actor 20 times. Every time it came back with its memory, its files
and its root filesystem exactly as it left them, sometimes on a different machine.

Then the real test. Three Claude Code agents, each a loop that asks Claude a question every 45
seconds and keeps a counter only in process memory. I suspended all three mid-loop and resumed
them. Each counter picked up at N+1, one agent landed on a different node, and all three kept
getting answers from Claude. A live Node.js process tree, frozen to a bucket and thawed somewhere
else, with no idea anything happened.

That's genuinely impressive, and it's the thing that makes the economics work.

## "Sub-500 ms resume" is true. For small agents.

In-cluster, with upstream's own Locust harness:

| Agent memory | Wake p50 (p95) | Sleep p50 |
|---|---|---|
| a few MB | 0.22 s (0.33 s) | 0.54 s |
| 1 GiB | 3.5 s (4.0 s) | 3.5 s |
| 2 GiB | 6.9 s (15 s) | 10 s |

A real coding agent holds 0.5 to 2 GB. Budget about three and a half seconds of wake-up per
gigabyte, expect a long tail past 1 GB, and know that most of it is copying the snapshot to and
from object storage.

Substrate also offers microVMs, a stronger isolation boundary than gVisor. At 1 GB they woke
just as fast. At 2 GB they took 16 seconds against gVisor's 7, and the extra time was the
microVM restore itself.

Two things soften this. Resume time barely moved under load: 15 agents cycling on 10 workers, 2,123
requests, zero failures. And there's a "pause" mode that keeps the snapshot on the node's local
disk. It woke a 1 GiB agent in 0.9 s instead of 3.5 s.

## The security story is half right

The good half: Substrate can inject API keys at its egress gateway. I put a random secret in a
Kubernetes Secret, had the agent call out with a placeholder, and the upstream server received
the real key. Then I searched the agent's environment, every process's `/proc` environ and its
whole filesystem. Not there. Egress is deny-by-default, DNS included, and the allow-list works.

The other half: **memory snapshots are not encrypted.** They're zstd-compressed RAM in a bucket.
The upstream Claude Code demo passes the API key as an environment variable, so I scanned its
snapshots. The full key was in there 77 times.

So read access to the snapshot bucket is read access to every secret any agent ever held in
memory. The fix exists and works (inject credentials, don't hand them to the agent), but nothing
stops you from doing it the easy way, and the official demo does it the easy way.

## The rough edges

- The Claude Code demo can't actually reach Claude. Substrate blocks all egress for an actor with
  no policy, and the demo doesn't create one. Secure default, stale demo. One rule fixes it.
- Everything builds from source on your laptop, including a Rust module. On an M-series Mac
  that's amd64 under emulation: 16 minutes for the first install, three attempts to get it
  through.
- When a worker pod dies, its agents go to CRASHED and wait for a manual revert. Plan around
  that if you want spot nodes.
- Alpine-based agents couldn't resolve ordinary names like `example.com` inside the sandbox.
  The fully-qualified form (`example.com.`, trailing dot) works. Node-based agents were fine.

I've written all of these up with reproduction steps for the maintainers.

## Is it worth it?

It comes down to one number: how much of the time your agents are actually awake.

For 1,000 agents at half a vCPU and 1 GB each, always-on pods need about 128 nodes, roughly
$20k a month on-demand. If agents are awake 5% of the time, Substrate needs about 14 nodes,
roughly $2.3k. At 25% awake the saving is 2x. At 50% it's gone. Snapshot storage is a rounding
error either way.

Then I priced the hosted alternatives, and this part surprised me. E2B and Daytona bill per
second only while a sandbox runs; a paused one costs nothing. For the same 1,000 agents at 5%
awake that's about $1.5k a month, cheaper than Substrate on on-demand nodes at every duty cycle
I modelled, because you pay for exactly the awake time with no headroom and no control plane.
Substrate only comes out cheapest on spot nodes (about $1.1k), which I didn't test. So the
reason to run it yourself is control, not price: your VPC, your egress rules, your data staying
put.

My take:

- **A handful of agents, or busy ones?** Don't bother. A Deployment is simpler.
- **Hundreds of stateful, mostly-idle agents, one per user or customer?** This is the most
  credible open-source answer I've seen, and the snapshot/restore core is solid today.
- **Production this quarter?** Not yet. It's pre-1.0 and ships weekly. Prototype on it, and
  adopt the credential-injection pattern now whatever runtime you use.

The repo has the setup script, every test, the raw benchmark data and a verified teardown.
If you run it on different hardware, I'd like to see your numbers.

https://github.com/shivanathd/agent-substrate-field-test

Source material

The repo's write-ups as raw Markdown, for detail beyond the drafts.

docs/findings.md
# Findings

Agent Substrate @ `main` (2026-10-16, after v0.5.0), GKE 1.36.4, 2× c3-standard-4, gVisor.
Every claim below links to a script in `tests/` and a raw log in `results/raw/`.

## Summary

| # | Claim we tested | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Actor state survives suspend/resume | **Holds.** 20/20 cycles, memory + file + rootfs counters exact | `tests/01-state-persistence.sh` |
| F2 | An actor can resume on any worker | **Holds.** 20 cycles landed on all 3 workers, state intact | same |
| F1b | Resume is sub-500 ms | **Holds for a small actor.** Resume overhead p50 0.27 s, p95 0.34 s (first request minus warm request) | same |
| F3 | Real coding agents can be suspended mid-life and resumed | **Holds.** 3 Claude Code agents; every agent's in-memory loop counter continued after resume and Claude kept answering | `tests/03-claude-multiplex.sh` |
| F5 | Credentials are injected outside the agent's reach | **Holds.** 8/8 incl. controls | `tests/05-credential-injection.sh` |
| F6 | — (not claimed) Secrets in RAM end up in snapshots | **Yes, in plaintext.** API key found 77× across 12 snapshot objects | `tests/06-snapshot-secret-scan.py` |

## F1 / F2 — state persistence and migration

Upstream counter demo, 20 cycles of: request (wakes actor) → request (warm) → suspend.

| | p50 | p95 | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| First request after suspend (incl. wake) | 0.907 s | 0.990 s | 1.018 s |
| Warm request | 0.642 s | 0.697 s | 0.839 s |
| **Resume overhead** (first − warm) | **0.269 s** | **0.336 s** | 0.345 s |

The absolute numbers include India → us-west1 plus a `kubectl port-forward` tunnel; the
difference is the wake cost. Server-side numbers from the in-cluster benchmark are in
[benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md).

The operator-side "suspend" column (~8.5 s) is **not** a suspend latency: it is dominated by
`kubectl ate` opening a fresh port-forward for every status poll. Don't quote it.

## F3 — Claude Code agents

Three upstream demo agents, each a shell loop calling `claude --print` every 45 s with a TICK
counter held only in process memory. After suspending all three and resuming them:

| Agent | Tick at suspend | Tick after resume | Claude answered after resume |
|---|---|---|---|
| luna | 23 | 26 | yes — resumed on a **different worker pod** |
| mars | 22 | 25 | yes |
| orion | 24 | 28 | yes |

Result 8/8 (`results/raw/03-claude-multiplex-*.log`). Placement is the scheduler's choice: across
the three runs we made, 1, 2 and 0 of 3 agents moved pods, always with ticks intact. Each
suspend or resume, as seen from the CLI, took 3.7–5.1 s end to end for a ~100 MB Claude Code
process tree (this includes CLI tunnel setup from India; see benchmarks for server-side time).

Two things the upstream demo gets wrong today:

1. **It never answers.** Substrate denies all egress, DNS included, for an actor with no
   `EgressPolicy` (`"Actor has no egress policy; blocking all DNS queries"`), and the demo
   creates none. Every `claude` call fails with `EAI_AGAIN`. One `tls_passthrough` rule for
   `api.anthropic.com:443` per agent fixes it. Secure default; stale demo.
2. **"Two pods for three agents" is not how placement works now.** A worker reports capacity of
   `0/1000` actors, `3920m` CPU, `~13.6 GB` memory. With 2 GiB agents ~6 fit per worker, so the
   third agent did not wait for a pod — it was packed beside the first. Density comes from
   bin-packing plus suspension, not one actor per pod.

## F5 — egress credential injection and policy

A random secret in a Kubernetes Secret; actor sends `Authorization: placeholder`.

- PASS upstream received `Bearer <secret>`; never saw the placeholder
- PASS upstream saw the request from the **egress gateway pod IP**
- PASS secret absent from the actor's env, every `/proc/*/environ`, and a full filesystem grep
- PASS HTTPS to a host the policy does not cover is refused
- PASS **control:** the same HTTPS request succeeds once a `tls_passthrough` rule allows it

### DNS quirk found while building the control

Inside the gVisor sandbox (Alpine/musl), names resolved through the search-domain list fail:
`wget https://example.com/` → `bad address`, `getent hosts example.com` → nothing, while
`nslookup example.com` and the fully-qualified `https://example.com./` work. Upstream's resolver
appears to answer search-domain expansions (`example.com.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` …, `ndots:5`)
in a way musl treats as fatal. glibc clients (Node, in the Claude agents) were unaffected.
**Workaround:** trailing-dot FQDNs, or `ndots:1` in the actor's resolv.conf.

## F6 — secrets in memory snapshots

`MEMORY`-fidelity snapshots are the actor's RAM, zstd-compressed (format: `ATESPRSE` magic,
4-byte version, zstd stream) and written to the bucket. **Not encrypted by Substrate**; only
the object store's default at-rest encryption applies.

The demo passes `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as an env var (it is also stored in the ActorTemplate, i.e.
in Substrate's Postgres). Scanning 12 snapshot objects found the full key **77 times**: in the
template's golden image (8–52× per object), in each actor's incremental page delta (5×), and in
checkpoint metadata (1×).

**Implication:** read access to the snapshot bucket = read access to every secret any agent
ever held in memory. Mitigations, in order:

1. Don't put secrets in actors. Use egress credential injection (F5) — it works.
2. Treat the snapshot bucket as a secret store: CMEK, no broad `storage.objectViewer`,
   access logging, retention limits.
3. Short-lived tokens only, if an agent must hold one.

## Install and operations

| Finding | Detail |
|---|---|
| Everything is built from source on the operator's machine | Go images via `ko`, Envoy dataplane via Docker incl. a Rust dynamic module. No prebuilt-image path in the quickstart. First install 16 min. |
| Apple silicon is slow and fragile | amd64 images build under emulation. Two concurrent builds (kind + GKE) made `apt-get` inside a build time out; serial builds worked. |
| 60 s readiness timeouts | First install on a slow link fails while images are still pulling; a rerun succeeds. |
| GKE bootstrap is good | `setup-gcp bootstrap` produced cluster + bucket + IAM + dashboards in 6 min, no edits. |
| No managed install of the benchmark harness | Upstream automation assumes a second orchestration cluster; we render its Job template directly (`bench/run-locust.py`). |
docs/use-cases.md
# Use cases — where Agent Substrate fits, and where it doesn't

The shape Substrate is built for: **many agents, each with real state, each idle most of the
time.** If your agents are stateless, or you have ten of them, a plain Deployment (or one VPS)
is simpler and you should stop reading here.

## Good fits

### 1. One persistent coding agent per engineer or per ticket
A Claude Code / Codex sandbox per person that keeps its checkout, installed toolchain, shell
history and running processes for days, but costs nothing while nobody is typing.

- **Tested:** F3 — three Claude Code agents suspended mid-loop and resumed (sometimes on another
  worker) with their process memory intact, still answering.
- **Watch:** a real coding agent holds 0.5–2 GB. See B2 in [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md) for
  how suspend/resume time grows with memory.

### 2. A dormant agent per customer, user or recruiter
Thousands of agents, each with its own memory and files, woken by a webhook, a Slack message or a
schedule. The density math is the whole point: idle agents cost snapshot storage, not RAM.

- **Tested:** F1/F2 — counter state exact over 20 cycles across 3 workers; resume overhead
  p95 0.34 s for a small actor.
- **Cost:** an idle Claude Code agent's own snapshot delta was ~300 KB on top of an ~18 MB
  per-template base. See [cost.md](cost.md).

### 3. Running untrusted, agent-written code
gVisor (or microVM) isolation per actor, default-deny egress, and an allow-list per actor.

- **Tested:** F5 — uncovered egress refused, allowed egress works, DNS is blocked entirely for an
  actor with no policy.

### 4. Keeping API keys out of the agent
The egress gateway injects credentials into outbound requests, so the agent never holds them.

- **Tested:** F5 — upstream got the real token; the token was nowhere in the actor's env, `/proc`
  or filesystem.
- **This matters more than it looks:** F6 showed that anything an agent *does* hold in RAM is
  written in plaintext to every memory snapshot.

### 5. RL / eval fleets
Thousands of short-lived environments forked from a golden snapshot. Each template already
builds a golden snapshot, and actors start from it.

- **Not tested here.** Upstream's `sweperf` benchmark targets this; see B4.

## Poor fits

| Situation | Why | Use instead |
|---|---|---|
| < ~50 agents, or always-busy agents | No idle time to multiplex; you pay the operational cost for nothing | A Deployment, or one VM |
| You don't run Kubernetes | It is a Kubernetes add-on with its own Postgres, router, gateway and node agent | Hosted sandboxes (E2B, Modal, Daytona) |
| You need it production-ready this quarter | Pre-1.0, weekly releases, APIs explicitly unstable | Watch it; prototype on it |
| Agents must hold long-lived secrets | Memory snapshots will contain them (F6) | Egress injection, or don't snapshot memory |
docs/cost.md
# Cost

Prices are GCP list prices for `us-west1`, pulled from the Cloud Billing Catalog API on
2026-10-16 (pd-balanced and GCS operations from the public price page). Your discounts differ.

| Item | Price |
|---|---|
| C3 vCPU / GiB RAM, on-demand | $0.03465 / h, $0.003938 / h |
| → `c3-standard-4` (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) | **$0.2016 / h** on-demand, $0.0795 / h spot |
| pd-balanced boot disk (100 GB per node) | ~$0.10 / GB-month → $0.0137 / h per node |
| GKE cluster management fee | $0.10 / h (one zonal cluster per billing account is credited) |
| GCS Standard storage | $0.020 / GB-month |
| GCS Class A operations | $0.005 / 1,000 |

## What this field test cost

Test cluster: 2 nodes + disks + fee ≈ **$0.53 / h ≈ $12.73 / day**.

| | Hours | Approx. cost |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster up, install → end of benchmarks | ~4 | ~$2.10 |
| Container registry + snapshot bucket (a few GB, one day) | — | < $0.10 |
| Anthropic API (3 agents × one-sentence prompts × ~1 h) | — | < $1 |
| **Total** | | **~$3** |
| Leaving it running afterwards | per day | $12.73 |

The expensive resource in this test was **time**, not money: ~45–60 min to stand up from
nothing on a laptop, most of it image builds (see [timeline.md](timeline.md)).

## What it would cost to run agents on it

### Inputs we measured

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Snapshot of an idle Claude Code agent | **~300 KB** own delta + **~18 MB** base shared per template (97 MB raw RAM) | F6 scan, GCS listing |
| Snapshots of deleted actors | removed with the actor — nothing orphaned | GCS listing after benchmarks |
| Worker capacity per `c3-standard-4` | 3.92 vCPU, ~13 GiB allocatable, 1,000-actor cap | `kubectl ate get workers` |
| Wake latency (gVisor, p50) | ~0.2 s small; ~3.5 s at 1 GiB; ~6.9 s at 2 GiB (microVM: 16 s) | [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md) |

### Model: 1,000 agents, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GiB each when awake

- **Always on** (one pod per agent): bounded by CPU → **128 nodes ≈ $20,200 / month**.
- **Substrate**, agents awake 5% of the time, 2× headroom for bursts: 100 concurrently awake →
  13 nodes + 1 for the control plane → **14 nodes ≈ $2,270 / month**, plus snapshot storage
  (< $4 / month even with no dedupe) and GCS operations (~$30 / month at 20 wakes per agent
  per day).

| Agents awake | Nodes (vs 128 always-on) | Saving |
|---|---|---|
| 5% | 14 | **9.1×** |
| 10% | 27 | 4.7× |
| 25% | 65 | 2.0× |
| 50% | 129 | none |

**The whole case rests on duty cycle.** Below ~25% awake, Substrate is substantially cheaper;
by ~50% it is not. Storage and API costs are rounding errors next to compute.

### Against hosted sandboxes

Same 1,000 agents at 0.5 vCPU / 1 GiB, billed per second while awake. Monthly, list prices
read 2026-10-16 (see Sources in the report). Substrate rows include ~$30/month of GCS.

| Option | 5% awake | 10% | 25% | 50% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Substrate, on-demand nodes | $2,303 | $4,347 | $10,319 | $20,378 |
| Substrate, spot nodes (untested) | $1,056 | $1,941 | $4,527 | $8,882 |
| E2B or Daytona (identical rates; not billed while paused) | $1,511 | $3,022 | $7,556 | $15,111 |
| Vercel Sandbox (incl. $0.08/GB-month snapshots) | $3,190 | $6,300 | $15,629 | $31,178 |
| Always-on pods, one per agent | $20,191 | $20,191 | $20,191 | $20,191 |

- **A hosted sandbox that stops billing when paused beats Substrate on on-demand nodes at every
  duty cycle we modelled.** It pays for exactly the awake time, with no 2× headroom and no
  control-plane node. E2B documents pause at ~4 s per GiB and resume at ~1 s (vendor figures).
- **Substrate on spot nodes is the cheapest option**, 30–40% under E2B/Daytona. Spot was not
  tested; a reclaimed node CRASHes its actors until reverted.
- The reasons to self-host are mostly not price: data residency, VPC and egress control, your own
  models and quotas, and no per-vendor limits. Count the operating cost (Postgres, router,
  gateway, node agents, upgrades on a pre-1.0 project) before choosing on price.
- Daytona's disk beyond 5 GiB per sandbox ($0.000108/GiB-hour) and E2B's plan fees are excluded.

### What the model leaves out

- **Wake latency is the price you pay.** A 1 GiB agent takes ~3.5 s to wake. If users wait on it,
  that is a product cost the spreadsheet doesn't show.
- **Operations.** Postgres, router, egress gateway and a node agent are yours to run, upgrade
  and page on. Pre-1.0 means breaking changes.
- **Spot nodes** cut the node price ~60% ($0.0795 vs $0.2016/h) and suit this workload well,
  since actors already live in snapshots — but a reclaimed node CRASHes the actors on it
  (see B6 in [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md)) and they need a revert. Not tested.
- **Committed-use discounts** would shrink both columns equally.
docs/benchmarks.md
# Benchmarks

Upstream's own Locust harness (`benchmarking/locust`), running **in-cluster** as a Job, so these
are cluster-local numbers with no laptop or WAN in the path. Each row is an upstream catalogue
entry (`benchmarking/automation/tests.yaml`) run unmodified; `bench/run-all.sh` only groups them
and redeploys the workload shape each group needs. Summary: `results/benchmarks.csv`; raw runs:
`results/raw/bench/`.

**Cluster:** 2× `c3-standard-4` (7.84 vCPU, 25.9 GB allocatable), GKE 1.36.4, gVisor, GCS in
the same region. Upstream's `glutton` workload: a small Go server that can hold, churn and
re-read a configurable amount of memory. Each benchmark actor reserves 1 vCPU.

**How to read the operations**

- **Suspend**: checkpoint the sandbox → upload the snapshot to object storage → free the worker.
- **Resume**: fetch manifest → download snapshot → restore the sandbox on any worker.
- **Pause / resume-from-pause**: checkpoint to the *node's local disk* (no upload); the next
  resume is steered back to that node. Cheaper, but the actor stays pinned to the node.

## B1 — floor latency, one small actor

| Run | n | Resume p50 / p95 / p99 | Suspend p50 / p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `glutton_baseline_1_user` (run 1) | 33 | 220 / 330 / 350 ms | 540 / 640 ms |
| `glutton_baseline_1_user` (run 2) | 33 | 210 / 340 / 380 ms | 510 / 640 ms |
| `glutton_baseline_1_user_pause` | 46 | **130 / 140 / 140 ms** (from pause) | — |

Where the time goes (server-side phase breakdown, p50):

| Resume ≈ 205 ms | | Suspend ≈ 440 ms | |
|---|---|---|---|
| manifest fetch (GCS) | 31 ms | sandbox checkpoint (gVisor) | 118 ms |
| snapshot download (GCS) | 47 ms | **snapshot upload (GCS)** | **315 ms** |
| sandbox restore (gVisor) | 122 ms | other | ~5 ms |

**The "sub-500 ms resume" claim holds for small actors**, with margin at p99. Object storage is
~40% of resume and ~70% of suspend.

## B2 — memory size is the dominant factor

Upstream's memory entries run for 1 minute, which fits only 1–7 cycles of a multi-GiB actor. We
ran the same entries, same flags, for **5 minutes** (`*_5m` in the results) and report those; the
1-minute runs are listed for comparison.

| Resident memory | Run | Wakes measured | Wake p50 / p95 / p99 | Sleep p50 / p95 | Wake from pause p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| few MB | `glutton_baseline_1_user` | 33 | 0.22 / 0.33 / 0.35 s | 0.54 / 0.64 s | 0.13 s |
| 1 GiB | `glutton_mem_1gi_gvisor_5m` | 36 | **3.5 / 4.0 / 4.5 s** | 3.5 / 4.2 s | 0.92 s (1-min run) |
| 2 GiB | `glutton_mem_2gi_gvisor_5m` | 13 | **6.9 / 15 / 15 s** | 10 / 18 s | — |
| *1 GiB, 1-min* | `glutton_mem_1gi_gvisor` | 7 | 3.2 / 3.7 s | 3.5 / 3.7 s | |
| *2 GiB, 1-min* | `glutton_mem_2gi_gvisor` | 3 | 7.3 s | 9.5 s | |

| Phase (gVisor, p50) | few MB | 1 GiB | 2 GiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| snapshot download | 0.05 s | 2.31 s | 4.96 s |
| sandbox restore | 0.12 s | 1.03 s | 1.77 s |
| sandbox checkpoint | 0.12 s | 0.85 s | 5.90 s |
| snapshot upload | 0.33 s | 2.44 s | 3.93 s |

- **Budget ~3.5 s of wake per GiB**, and a heavy tail past 1 GiB: at 2 GiB one wake in twenty
  took 15 s. A real coding agent sits at 0.5–2 GiB, so plan in seconds, not milliseconds.
- Transfer to and from object storage is about two thirds of wake time at 1 GiB.
- **Pause** avoids the transfer: 3.5× faster wake at 1 GiB. Use it for short idle gaps;
  suspend for long ones (it frees the node).
- `--mem-read all` makes the actor touch all of its memory after every wake, so this is the
  worst case for lazy page loading.

## B3 — durable directories

An 8 MiB file in a durable directory (a volume Substrate persists with the actor), read back and
verified by SHA-256 after every resume. All three runs: 0 failures.

| Run | What's snapshotted | Resume p50 / p95 | Suspend p50 / p95 | First read after resume p50 / p95 | Warm read p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `durdir_data_baseline` | durable dir only, explicit resume | 250 / 290 ms | 610 / 720 ms | 83 / 100 ms | 59 ms |
| `durdir_implicit_resume` | same, **woken by the request itself** | — | 620 / 720 ms | **330 / 370 ms** (wake + read) | 58 ms |
| `durdir_full_baseline` | durable dir **and** memory | 370 / 540 ms | 1,400 / 1,800 ms | 67 / 110 ms | 54 ms |

- **Letting the router wake the actor costs nothing extra**: 330 ms for wake-plus-read equals an
  explicit resume (250) plus a read (83). Agents can simply be addressed; no wake RPC needed.
- The first read after a resume pays ~25 ms of lazy loading over a warm read.
- Snapshotting memory as well as the volume roughly doubles suspend time (upload: 0.46 s → 1.1 s).

## B5 — concurrency and oversubscription

| Run | Users / workers | Requests | Fail | Resume p50 / p95 / p99 | Suspend p50 / p95 | Upload p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `glutton_baseline_1_user` | 1 / 1 | 103 | 0 | 220 / 330 / 350 ms | 540 / 640 ms | 0.33 s |
| `glutton_baseline_5_users` | 5 / 5 | 469 | 0 | 230 / 290 / 340 ms | 560 / 1000 ms | 0.36 s |
| `glutton_baseline_10_users` | 10 / 10 | 793 | 0 | 250 / 330 / 370 ms | 820 / 1500 ms | 0.59 s |
| `glutton_oversubscribe_15_users` | **15 / 10** | **2,123** | **0** | 270 / 370 / 450 ms | 1400 / 2200 ms | 1.12 s |

- **Resume barely moves with load**; 1.5× oversubscription produced zero failures.
- **Suspend degrades with concurrency**, and almost all of it is upload: with 15 actors cycling,
  upload p50 goes from 0.33 s to 1.12 s. Two nodes' worth of egress to GCS is the bottleneck,
  not the scheduler.

## B6 — what happens when a worker disappears

Not a planned test: we observed it when a workload redeploy deleted a worker pod that was still
hosting three actors. All three went to **`ACTOR_STATE_CRASHED`** with
`"suspend failed: worker pod went away while hosting the actor"` (or `resume failed: …`).

- Recovery is not automatic. Upstream's CLI documents `kubectl ate revert actor …` to return a
  crashed actor to its last external snapshot; **we did not exercise revert** (our cleanup
  deleted these actors), so "nothing lost up to the last snapshot" is upstream's claim, not a
  measured result.
- Whatever an actor did after its last snapshot is, by construction, not in any snapshot.
- Implication for spot nodes or node upgrades: suspend actors before draining, or plan for
  reverts. Snapshot frequency is your recovery-point objective.

## microVM vs gVisor

Same catalogue entries with `sandboxClass: microvm` (Cloud Hypervisor via Kata, nested
virtualisation on the C3 nodes), 5-minute runs. All 0 failures.

| Memory | Sandbox | Wakes measured | Wake p50 / p95 / p99 | Sleep p50 / p95 | Download / restore (p50) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 GiB | gVisor | 36 | 3.5 / 4.0 / 4.5 s | 3.5 / 4.2 s | 2.31 / 1.03 s |
| 1 GiB | microVM | 23 | 3.5 / 4.1 / **8.4 s** | 3.7 / 4.3 s | 2.55 / 0.84 s |
| 2 GiB | gVisor | 13 | 6.9 / 15 / 15 s | 10 / 18 s | 4.96 / 1.77 s |
| 2 GiB | microVM | 8 | **16 / 17 / 17 s** | 11 / 13 s | 6.47 / **9.54 s** |

- **At 1 GiB the two are the same at the median**; microVM has the heavier tail (p99 8.4 s vs
  4.5 s, and an outlier of 9.4 s in the 1-minute run too).
- **At 2 GiB microVM wakes take more than twice as long**, and the difference is the sandbox
  restore itself (9.5 s vs 1.8 s), not the bucket. Choosing the stronger isolation boundary is
  cheap for small agents and expensive for big ones.
- 8 and 13 wakes are small samples; the 2 GiB medians are solid enough to act on, the p95s less so.
- First run of `install-microvm-deps.sh` needs a `zstd` binary and downloads 924 MB through the
  operator's machine (issue 8 in [upstream-issues.md](upstream-issues.md)).

## Harness notes

- Three runs were invalid: leftover actors from the previous test in the group filled the
  single worker and new actors got `no worker has room for the actor`. They are kept in
  `results/raw/bench-invalid/` with an explanation; `bench/run-locust.py` now cleans up between
  runs, and the reruns are what's reported.
- `server_summary.json` (cluster packing, PSI) is empty: it needs upstream's optional
  Prometheus stack, which we did not install.
- Upstream's runs are 1–2 minutes long. Good for latency percentiles, too short to say
  anything about drift, leaks or long-tail behaviour.
docs/methodology.md
# Methodology

## The question

> Can we run hundreds of **persistent, mostly-idle agents** (one per user/customer, each holding
> memory and files for days, active a few minutes an hour) on a handful of nodes — with resume
> fast enough that a person doesn't notice, and without losing state?

That is the workload Agent Substrate is built for. Every test below maps to one part of that
question. Pass/fail bars were written **before** any test ran.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Substrate | `agent-substrate/substrate` @ `main`, shallow clone 2026-10-16 (release v0.5.0 was 2026-10-14) |
| Cluster | GKE 1.36.4 zonal, `us-west1-c`, 2× `c3-standard-4` (4 vCPU / 16 GB), nested virtualisation on |
| Snapshot store | GCS, same region |
| Sandbox | gVisor (default); microVM (Cloud Hypervisor via Kata) where noted |
| Load generator | Upstream Locust harness, run as an in-cluster Job, so client latency is cluster-local |
| Operator | arm64 Mac, Docker Desktop 8 GB, India → us-west1 |

Everything is the upstream default unless stated. We did not tune anything.

## Tests

### Functional (does it do what it says?)

| ID | Test | Pass bar |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | State persistence: counter actor, 20 suspend → resume cycles via the router; memory, file and rootfs counters checked every cycle | 0 mismatches |
| F2 | Migration: same as F1, record which worker pod served each cycle | Actor observed on >1 worker with state intact |
| F3 | Claude Code multiplex: 3 real Claude Code agents on a 2-worker pool, upstream demo | All tasks complete; the waiting agent resumes with its workspace intact |
| F4 | Egress identity + policy: upstream egress demo | Allowed URL succeeds; disallowed URL is refused; non-actor client refused at mTLS |
| F5 | Credential injection: secret referenced by policy, injected at the gateway | Upstream call authenticated; the secret is absent from the actor's env, `/proc/*/environ` and filesystem |

### Benchmarks (how fast, how dense, what breaks?)

All via the upstream Locust tests in `benchmarking/locust/tests/`, results pulled as CSV.

| ID | Upstream test | Metric | What it answers | Bar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | `glutton.py` baseline, 1 user | p50/p95/p99 suspend, resume | Floor latency of a small actor | resume p95 < 1 s |
| B2 | `glutton.py` 1 GiB resident memory, gVisor vs microVM | suspend/resume vs memory size; snapshot bytes | Cost of a "fat" agent (a real coding agent holds 0.5–2 GB) | Measured, priced |
| B3 | `durdir.py` explicit vs implicit (traffic-triggered) resume | `ResumeActor`, `DurDirServeAfterResume` | Does the first request after wake pay a lazy-load penalty? | Measured |
| B4 | `sweperf.py` (replayed real SWE-Perf agent task, suspend between cycles) | `ResumeToFirstExec`, `TaskWallClock` | Overhead on a realistic coding-agent task | **Not run** — F3 (real Claude Code agents) covered the realistic case; sweperf images are large and out of time budget |
| B5 | Oversubscription: rising users vs workers, upstream catalogue | resume p95, suspend p95, failures | Where density stops being free | Met: 0 failures at 15 users / 10 workers |
| B6 | Node kill mid-run | actors recovered, data since last snapshot | Failure blast radius | **Not run deliberately.** Observed once by accident (worker pod deleted under 3 actors → CRASHED); revert not exercised |

Benchmarks that ran differently from this plan: the multi-GiB memory entries were also run for 5
minutes instead of upstream's 1 minute, because 1 minute fits only 1–7 cycles. Both are kept.

## Cost model

`cost per 1,000 idle agents / month` =
`(nodes needed for the active set × node $/h × 730)` + `snapshot GB × GCS $/GB-month` +
`GCS operations` + `GKE management fee`

…compared against the naive baseline of one always-on pod per agent at the same pod size.
Inputs come from B2 (snapshot bytes), B5 (active set per node) and the public GCP price list
for `us-west1` on the test date.

## What we deliberately did not test

- Multi-zone / regional HA, upgrades, or anything over multiple days.
- Production auth (OIDC/JWT providers) — the dev install uses ServiceAccount tokens.
- Scale beyond 2 nodes. Upstream's own scale claims ("millions of sandboxes") are theirs, not ours.

# Timeline — what actually happened

Wall-clock log of the field test, kept as it happened. Times are IST (UTC+5:30), 2026-10-16.
Identifiers are replaced with placeholders: `<PROJECT_ID>`, `<BILLING_ACCOUNT>`, `<ORG_ID>`.

Operator machine: Apple-silicon MacBook (arm64), Docker Desktop with 8 GB / 18 CPUs, on a home
connection in India. Cluster region: `us-west1-c`.

| Time | Step | Result | Elapsed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11:22 | Prereq check: gcloud 588, kubectl 1.34, Go 1.27, Docker 29.7 | gcloud user token expired; ADC fine | — |
| 11:30 | `gcloud auth login` | OK | ~1 min |
| 11:31 | Org-policy check (nested virt, resource locations) | No blockers | ~1 min |
| 11:33 | Create throwaway project, link billing, $50 budget alert | OK | ~2 min |
| 11:37 | `go run ./tools/setup-gcp bootstrap` (APIs, GKE 1.36.4, 2× c3-standard-4, GCS bucket, IAM, dashboards) | OK | **6 min** |
| 11:36 | Local: `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh` + `install-ate-kind.sh` (parallel with GKE) | FAIL — postgres rollout 60 s timeout while the image was still pulling | 19 min |
| 11:45 | GKE: `hack/install-ate.sh --deploy-ate-system --deploy-demo-counter` (attempt 1) | FAIL — `apt-get update` inside envoy-dataplane image build could not reach deb.debian.org | 15 min |
| 12:00 | Local retry | FAIL — `k8s-credential-provider` rollout timeout (images still pulling) | 11 min |
| 12:03 | GKE attempt 2 | FAIL — same apt error | 2 min |
| 12:05 | Isolated repro of the apt step via `docker buildx` | Passes in 24 s → failure correlated with concurrent local build saturating Docker | — |
| 12:06 | GKE attempt 3 (apt layer now cached) | **OK** | 16 min |
| 12:13 | Local retry 3 | FAIL — kind API server TLS handshake timeout (Docker Desktop saturated) | 3 min |
| 12:17 | Paused kind node to give the GKE build the whole Docker VM | — | — |
| 12:24 | `go install ./cmd/kubectl-ate`, router port-forward, smoke test | counter answers; 3 counters increment | 2 min |
| 12:26 | **F1/F2** `tests/01-state-persistence.sh` (20 cycles) | PASS 20/20, 3 workers | 5 min |
| 12:31 | Deploy sandbox + claude-code-multiplex demos | OK | 9 min |
| 12:35 | **F5** credential injection, first version | 7/7 — but two checks too weak | 2 min |
| 12:38 | Add controls; control fails → diagnose → musl/search-domain DNS quirk; use FQDN | PASS 8/8 | 8 min |
| 12:46 | **F3** Claude multiplex, first version | 3/5 — demo has no egress policy (DNS blocked), and a worker holds many actors | 6 min |
| 12:55 | F3 rewritten: per-agent `api.anthropic.com` policy; strict answer check; bash 3.2 fix | PASS (final run 8/8) | 25 min |
| 13:08 | **F6** snapshot secret scan | API key found 77× in 12 snapshot objects | 6 min |
| 13:13 | Locust image build (Go under emulation) + workload deploy | image 12 min; deploy failed on macOS bash 3.2 bug | 13 min |
| 13:20 | Scaled demo worker pools to 0 for clean benchmark nodes | node CPU requests 88% → 69% | 1 min |
| 13:26 | Patched `deploy.sh` locally; workloads deployed | OK | 2 min |
| 13:28 | First in-cluster benchmark (pipeline check) | Resume p50 220 ms, Suspend p50 540 ms, 0 failures | 3 min |
| 13:32 | `bench/run-all.sh` gVisor suite (5 groups, 11 catalogue runs) | OK, 0 failures except 3 durdir runs | 45 min |
| 13:50 | Diagnose durdir failures: leftover actors from earlier tests filled the 1-worker pool (harness bug, ours) | `run-locust.py` now cleans between runs | 5 min |
| 14:16 | `install-microvm-deps.sh` | FAIL after a 924 MB download — needs `zstd` CLI (undocumented) | 4 min |
| 14:20 | Clean rerun of the 3 durdir runs | 0 failures | 11 min |
| 14:33 | microVM deps with a `zstd -d` shim | FAIL — shim picked up a python3 without `zstandard`; 924 MB downloaded again | 4 min |
| 14:40 | microVM deps, shim pinned to the right interpreter (third 924 MB download) | OK | 7 min |
| 14:45 | microVM 1 GiB and 2 GiB (upstream 1-min entries) | OK; 2 GiB fit one wake | 13 min |
| 15:00 | Same memory entries for 5 min, gVisor and microVM | OK, 0 failures; 2 GiB microVM 16 s vs gVisor 6.9 s | 37 min |
| 15:40 | Docs, report, sanitise, verify | — | — |

**Totals:** first command 11:22 → last benchmark 15:37, about **4 h 15 min** of wall-clock. Of
that, roughly 1 h 30 min was image builds and asset downloads through the laptop, ~1 h was
benchmark runtime, and the rest was tests, diagnosis and fixes.

## Lessons so far

1. **The installer builds every image from source on the operator's machine** (Go via ko, plus
   Docker builds for the Envoy dataplane, including a Rust dynamic module). There is no
   prebuilt-image install path in the dev quickstart.
2. **On Apple silicon, those builds run amd64 under emulation.** The Rust compile is the long pole.
3. **Readiness timeouts are 60 s.** On a slow link the first install fails while images are
   still pulling; a rerun succeeds. Not a bug in Substrate, but every first-time user will hit it.
4. **Don't build for two clusters at once on one laptop.** Docker Desktop at 8 GB could not serve
   a kind cluster and an emulated Rust build at the same time.
5. **Every heavy step goes through the operator's laptop**: images are built there and pushed,
   and the microVM assets (924 MB) are downloaded there and re-uploaded to the bucket. On a home
   connection that is most of the wall-clock time. Run setup from a cloud VM in the same region
   and most of these minutes disappear.
6. **The local kind path never completed** on this Mac. It was paused at 12:17 to free resources
   for GKE and we did not return to it; the field test is GKE-only.
docs/upstream-issues.md
# Issues worth reporting upstream

Observed against `603e006` (2026-10-16). Not yet filed; each has enough to reproduce.

## 1. Memory snapshots are not encrypted by Substrate (security, docs)

`MEMORY`-fidelity snapshots are written as `ATESPRSE` + version + zstd, with no application-layer
encryption. Any secret in the actor's RAM is readable by anyone with read access to the bucket.
We found an API key 77 times across 12 objects (`tests/06-snapshot-secret-scan.py`).

**Ask:** document this prominently next to `snapshotConfig`, recommend egress credential
injection over env-var secrets, and consider optional per-atespace envelope encryption (CMEK).

## 2. claude-code-multiplex demo can never reach the API (demo)

The demo creates no `EgressPolicy`, and an actor without one has all egress *including DNS*
blocked (`"Actor has no egress policy; blocking all DNS queries"`). Every `claude` call fails with
`EAI_AGAIN`. The demo also bakes `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` into the ActorTemplate (stored in Postgres,
and in every snapshot — see #1).

**Ask:** create a `tls_passthrough` policy for `api.anthropic.com:443` per agent in the
installer, and switch the key to egress credential injection.

## 3. claude-code-multiplex README describes old placement (docs)

"Two pods for three agents … the third agent stays suspended until a pod opens up." Workers now
report capacity `0/1000` actors with CPU/memory bin-packing, so the third agent is placed beside
the first and nothing waits.

## 4. musl clients can't resolve names through search domains in the sandbox (bug?)

Alpine sandbox (`demos/sandbox`): `wget https://example.com/` → `bad address`; `getent hosts
example.com` → empty; but `nslookup example.com` works and `https://example.com./` (FQDN) works.
`resolv.conf` has `ndots:5` and six search domains pointing at `169.254.17.1`. glibc (Node)
clients are fine. Looks like the actor DNS proxy answers search-domain expansions in a way musl
treats as fatal (e.g. SERVFAIL/REFUSED rather than NXDOMAIN).

## 5. `benchmarking/workloads/deploy.sh` fails on macOS bash 3.2 (bug, one-line fix)

`"${FAKE_ATELET_ENV[@]}"` on an empty array under `set -u` → `unbound variable`. Fix:
`${FAKE_ATELET_ENV[@]+"${FAKE_ATELET_ENV[@]}"}` — see [upstream-patch-bash32.diff](upstream-patch-bash32.diff).

## 6. First install fails on slow links (UX)

Rollout waits are 60 s. Pulling `postgres:18-alpine` and others took ~3 min from India, so the
first `install-ate.sh` / `install-ate-kind.sh` fails and a rerun succeeds.

**Ask:** a `--wait-timeout` on install (the workloads script already has one), or pre-pull.

## 7. No prebuilt-image install path (UX)

Every install builds every image from source on the operator's machine (Go via ko, Envoy
dataplane via Docker, including a Rust dynamic module). On Apple silicon that is amd64 under
emulation: 16 min for a first install and 12 min for the Locust image. Published release images
would make the quickstart minutes, not tens of minutes.

## 8. `install-microvm-deps.sh` needs the `zstd` CLI on the operator machine (docs)

It downloads the 924 MB `kata-static` release to the laptop, then `tar` fails with
`unable to run program "zstd -d -qq"` if `zstd` isn't installed — after the full download.
Not listed in prerequisites. Check for it up front (and consider having the cluster fetch the
assets itself rather than round-tripping ~1 GB through the operator's connection).

## 9. Benchmark automation assumes a second cluster (docs)

`benchmarking/automation` drives runs from a separate orchestration cluster. Running one
catalogue entry against your own cluster is easy (render `runner-job.yaml.tmpl`, see
`bench/run-locust.py` here) but undocumented.
docs/code-review.md
# Code review

Independent read of all 14 scripts by a separate review agent (no edits, read-only checks: bash -n, py_compile, verify.sh), then fixes applied and re-verified.

Reviewed 2026-10-16. 23 findings (3 high, 9 medium, 10 low, 1 info); 22 fixed.

| Severity | File | Issue | Fix | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| high | `scripts/teardown.sh` | Loaded the upstream checkout's .ate-dev-env.sh after env.sh, so a pre-existing checkout's PROJECT_ID could win and --delete-project would delete that project. | Teardown pins the target from env.sh, refuses if the upstream env names a different project, and refuses any project without the purpose=substrate-field-test label setup.sh applies. | fixed |
| high | `scripts/setup.sh` | Silently reused an existing project with the same ID, and re-pinned, patched and overwrote an existing substrate checkout. | Refuses an existing project without its label; clones into .upstream/substrate by default and refuses a checkout it did not create (marker file). | fixed |
| high | `tests/01, 03, 05` | State-polling loops had no timeout. A stuck actor hung the test forever; in test 03 that leaves three agents calling the Anthropic API every 45 s. | Every wait has a deadline (120-180 s) and fails instead of hanging. | fixed |
| medium | `tests/01, 03, 05` | set -e exits skipped cleanup, leaving actors, egress policies or running agents behind. | trap cleanup EXIT in each test; test 03's trap suspends all agents. | fixed |
| medium | `tests/05` | Replaced the shared credential-provider namespace-policy ConfigMap and never restored it; left two namespaces behind. | Backs the ConfigMap up first and restores it (or deletes ours) on exit; removes both namespaces. | fixed |
| medium | `scripts/teardown.sh` | Any unrecognised flag fell through to a full teardown. | Unknown options exit 2 before doing anything. | fixed |
| medium | `scripts/teardown.sh` | Printed 'project deleted' even if the delete failed; verify counted a gcloud error as zero resources and skipped Artifact Registry. | Delete failure exits 1; listings that error show ERR and fail verification; Artifact Registry repositories are checked. | fixed |
| medium | `scripts/verify.sh` | A failed rebuild left the old files in place so the lineage check still passed; on real drift it overwrote the originals. | A rebuild failure is a FAIL; originals are restored after comparison so verify never changes the repo. | fixed |
| medium | `bench/run-locust.py` | A timed-out Job kept running into the next test; the first pod failure was read as Job failure despite retries. | Waits on the Job's Complete/Failed condition; deletes a timed-out Job. | fixed |
| medium | `bench/run-locust.py` | Reported OK when stats.jsonl never arrived. | OK requires a Complete Job and a stats.jsonl on disk. | fixed |
| medium | `scripts/setup.sh` | grep -q under pipefail could break gcloud's pipe and create a duplicate budget. | grep -x > /dev/null instead of -q. | fixed |
| medium | `scripts/setup.sh` | go install may put kubectl-ate outside PATH; every test then fails. | Checks and prints the PATH line to add. | fixed |
| low | `results/raw/05-*.log` | The published F5 log contained the (random, already deleted) injected test token. | Masked in the log; the test now masks it when printing. | fixed |
| low | `tests/05` | grep -qw treated the dots in an IP as wildcards. | grep -Fqw. | fixed |
| low | `bench/run-all.sh` | An unknown group name deleted the current workloads and redeployed with empty arguments. | Unknown groups are skipped before anything is deleted. | fixed |
| low | `scripts/setup.sh` | Silently skipped the bash 3.2 patch when it no longer applied. | Distinguishes applied / already applied / no longer applies, and says which. | fixed |
| low | `tests/03` | Python 3.9/3.10 fromisoformat rejects Go's variable-length fractional seconds. | Parses whole seconds with strptime and adds the fraction. | fixed |
| low | `report/build_report.py` | Crashed if the oversubscription run was missing. | Guarded. | fixed |
| low | `bench/summarize.py, tests/*` | Wrote output relative to the current directory. | Paths are relative to the repo; tests cd to the repo root. | fixed |
| low | `scripts/sanitize.py, scripts/verify.sh` | --replace without '=' crashed (an empty OLD would corrupt files); a trailing --forbid tripped set -u. | Both validated with a clear error. | fixed |
| low | `bench/run-all.sh` | An unknown group name was skipped only after the run log was created, leaving an empty results/raw/bench-run-all-*.log behind (found by the runtime verify pass). | Group names are validated before anything is written; a typo exits 2. | fixed |
| low | `scripts/verify.sh` | The identity scan walked whole directories, so a local gitignored scripts/env.sh failed it, and tail -5 hid problems past the fifth. | Scans only files git would publish (git ls-files -co --exclude-standard) and shows up to 20 problems. | fixed |
| info | `scripts/setup.sh` | setup.sh has never been run end to end; it was assembled from steps that were each run individually during the field test. | Stated in the README. A clean-room run is the next validation step. | open |

_Generated by `report/build_report.py` from `docs/code-review.json`._
